notes.meaning: Paul introduces himself as an apostle, a messenger chosen and sent by God's own will. His mission is to proclaim the promise of true, eternal life found only in Christ Jesus. Facing death in a Roman prison, Paul looks beyond his earthly chains to the everlasting life God guarantees.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars suggest that 2 Timothy was written after Paul's death by a later follower using his name, because the vocabulary and writing style differ from Paul's earlier letters.

notes.meaning: Paul writes with deep affection to Timothy, calling him his beloved spiritual child. He prays for Timothy to receive grace, peace, and special mercy from God the Father and Christ Jesus. Ministers carrying heavy burdens need the steady help of God's mercy in every difficulty.

Paul gives thanks to God, whom he serves with a clear and honest conscience, just as his Jewish ancestors did. Even while locked away in chains, he regularly remembers Timothy in his prayers both day and night. Faithful believers can pray for their friends even when other work is stopped.

Paul vividly remembers the tears Timothy wept when they last said goodbye. Facing execution, the apostle deeply yearns to see his dear friend one more time. Being reunited with Timothy would fill Paul's heart with great joy.

Paul is comforted by the genuine faith he sees in Timothy, a sincere trust that is not just put on for show. This same faith lived first in Timothy's grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice, who taught him God's word. A family legacy of faith is a wonderful foundation, but each person must trust God for themselves.

Paul reminds Timothy to stir up the spiritual gift God gave him, comparing it to blowing on dying embers to build up a fire. God gave Timothy this divine power for ministry when Paul placed his hands on him. Believers must actively exercise the gifts God gives them so their zeal does not grow cold.

differ.view: Believers should seek the laying on of hands to receive spiritual gifts and must actively stir up these gifts, such as prophecy, rather than passively waiting for a new blessing.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Paul's laying on of hands refers to the sacrament of Holy Orders, which imprints an indelible spiritual character and gives permanent grace to serve as a church leader.

notes.meaning: God did not give His people a spirit of cowardice or timidity that shrinks back from danger. Instead, the Holy Spirit gives strength to face hardship, love that drives out fear, and self-control that keeps the mind calm. Christians can face trials with quiet courage because God provides what they lack.

Paul urges Timothy not to feel ashamed of telling others about the Lord Jesus, or of Paul being held as a prisoner for Christ. Instead, Timothy must be willing to suffer for the gospel alongside Paul. God Himself provides the strength needed to endure whatever trouble comes.

God rescued believers and called them to live holy lives set apart for Him. He did not do this because of any good deeds we have done, but according to His own purpose and grace. God planned this unearned favor in Christ Jesus before the world even began.

God's eternal plan became clearly visible when Jesus Christ our Savior came to earth. By His life, death, and resurrection, Jesus destroyed the power of death and made the way to immortal life crystal clear through the gospel. Death is no longer a hopeless end for those who trust in Christ.

Paul explains that God appointed him to proclaim this good news as a public herald, an apostle, and a teacher. He was given authority to carry the message to the Gentile nations and explain its truths to them. Proclaiming God's truth was the central calling of his life.

Paul explains that his preaching is the very reason he is currently suffering in chains, yet he feels no shame. He personally knows the faithful Savior he trusts and is fully confident that God can safely guard what has been placed in His hands until the final day of judgment. Knowing Christ personally gives believers unwavering peace in hard times.

Timothy is told to hold firmly to the model of sound, healthy teaching he heard directly from Paul. He must keep this truth safe while walking in the faith and love that come from Jesus. Standing up for God's truth must always be done with a loving heart toward others.

Paul commands Timothy to protect the precious treasure of the gospel that has been entrusted to his care. Human strength alone is not enough to guard God's truth from false teachers. Timothy must rely on the Holy Spirit who lives inside all true believers to keep it safe.

Paul shares the painful news that almost all the believers from the province of Asia abandoned him during his imprisonment. Among those who turned away were Phygelus and Hermogenes. In the Roman world, standing by a prisoner brought great danger, and many gave in to fear.

Paul asks the Lord to show special mercy to the household of Onesiphorus. In sharp contrast to those who fled, Onesiphorus repeatedly visited Paul, comforted him, and was never ashamed of his prison chains. True Christian friends stand with each other when times are hard.

When Onesiphorus arrived in Rome, he searched tirelessly through the crowded city until he found where Paul was locked up. Finding a prisoner in a vast imperial capital took great effort and carried real risk. His devoted love moved him to seek out his suffering brother without giving up.

Paul prays that the Lord will grant Onesiphorus mercy on the great day of judgment. Timothy was already well aware of the many ways this faithful man had served Paul back in Ephesus. Any reward believers receive from God on that final day comes through pure grace, not human merit.

differ.view: Some Anglicans hold that because Onesiphorus was likely dead, Paul's words show that limited, loving prayers for the departed can be allowable.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Because Paul mentions only Onesiphorus's household earlier and prays for him to receive mercy at the final judgment, many believe Onesiphorus had already died, providing biblical support for praying for the deceased.
